source.author: Agnivesa's Caraka Samhita, trans. Ram Karan Sharma & Bhagwan Dash
source.title: Caraka Samhita: Sarira Sthana, with English translation and commentary based on Cakrapani Datta's Ayurveda Dipika

method: Read ch.4 of the Sarira Sthana volume (paragraphs 34-40, its section on the doshas of body and mind and the classification of mental types) and ch.6 (paragraphs 5-7, on keeping the body's elements in balance), retrieved as a partial text extraction of a large scanned PDF - the extraction is real but has OCR noise throughout (garbled diacritics, occasional dropped words), so every claim below was checked against a passage clear enough to paraphrase confidently, and no Sanskrit terms are quoted verbatim from the noisy transliteration. This is the classical, primary-source origin of the sattva/rajas/tamas mental-type framework guna.json already uses via Frawley's (secondary, practitioner) treatment of it - the first primary classical text in Nimai's knowledge base for the guna content specifically.

claims.paraphrase: The text names three physical doshas - vata, pitta and kapha - as what vitiates the body, and two mental doshas - rajas and tamas - as what vitiates the mind. Disease is described as arising from vitiation of one or the other; there is no disease, physical or mental, without it.

Mental faculty is described as being of three types: sattvika, free of defect and marked by auspiciousness; rajasa, defective because it promotes a wrathful disposition; and tamasa, defective because it arises from ignorance. Each of the three is said to have innumerable further variation depending on the individual's body, circumstances and interactions, so what follows are illustrative categories, not an exhaustive list.

The sattvika type is further divided into seven illustrative subtypes, each named for and sharing traits with a different classical figure (among them Brahma, a sage-like Arsha type, and types associated with Indra, Varuna, Kubera and Gandharva). The Brahma-associated type is named as the purest of the seven, marked by purity, love of truth, self-control, discrimination, freedom from anger and jealousy, and goodwill extended equally to all beings.

The rajasa type is further divided into six illustrative subtypes, similarly named for different figures. One, the Asura-associated type, combines real bravery with cruelty, envy and a tendency toward self-praise; another, the Rakshasa-associated type, shows intolerance, constant anger and cruelty toward those weaker than itself. The subtypes vary, but share the same underlying wrathful, self-focused quality.

The tamasa type is further divided into three illustrative subtypes, named for animal, fish and plant life respectively. They share a lack of discrimination and intelligence, indulgence (food, sleep or passion) without restraint, and in the plant-associated type specifically, a marked deficiency across the intellectual faculties generally.

Whatever increases one element of the body reduces the element with the opposite qualities, and it is the qualities that matter, not the substance: two liquids can have opposite effects if their qualities differ. Treatment therefore works by applying the opposite quality - reducing what has increased and building up what has decreased - and stops once balance is back, because continuing would push the balance the other way.

Even healthy people should keep their balance through daily choices: after food dominated by one quality, follow it with a regimen of the opposite kind - for example, exercise after sweet, heavy food that raises kapha - but not to excess, since overdoing the correction creates its own imbalance.
